newsitem.title: UK: New firm targets criminals through computer clues.
newsitem.headline: New firm targets criminals through computer clues.

text.p: Computers hold the key to most frauds but state-of-the-art technology and expertise are needed to net the fraudsters, a new firm specialising in probing and analysing the information contained on them said on Friday.

"Just about every accountancy related fraud involves a computer of some form, whether it be a portable computer, a personal organiser or a main frame," Tim Allen, a director of newly-formed Computer Forensic Investigations told Reuters.
Allen, who has been involved in fraud investigation for the last 10 years, is co-founder of forensic accountancy firm Lee & Allen which has linked up with Computer Forensics for the new venture.

Using technology developed by Computer Forensics, the new firm is able to extract a copy of the hard disk, making sure the original computer under scrutiny can continue to be used as evidence as it is not corrupted or affected in any way.

This equipment -- known as a "portable evidence recovery unit" or PERU for short -- has been widely used by British police forces and tested in several prosecutions, Peter Verreck, a founder of Computer Forensic and a director of the new firm, told Reuters.
Once the information has been copied onto the computer, it is processed through a "forensic work station" where it can be analysed.

The system has been used on numerous cases and is not limited to probing frauds such as the collapse of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International but has been used in murder, blackmail, counterfeiting and child pornography inquiries.

"The unsophisticated fraudster gets a tip off they are being investigated and the first thing they will try and do is to erase the evidence and delete whatever files they can before anyone can get hold of their computer," Allen said.

But using the software at its disposal Computer Forensic can "recreate that very easily". "Even though they've gone through and deleted everything bit by bit, its very easy to bring that back up and see exactly what was there," he added.

This "forensic laboratory" enables the investigators to piece together the funds flow or money trail and piece together a civil or criminal action. "The key thing is to retain the evidential integrity of the data," Allen said.
One area which would not be immediately apparent without using the software is, the firm says, so-called "slack space".
These spaces are areas around computer files where information has been saved and then other data has been saved over the top, leaving parts of the original information behind.

Computer Forensic Investigations, which will have an initial staff of four but has a potential staff of 40 including Lee & Allen employees in New York and Hong Kong, is targeting lawyers and corporates.
"The focus is the commercial field in particular," Allen said. Verreck said the uniqueness of the service is the focus on computers, adding there are very few competitors in the market.
